pillar_reactions.evidence: Delivered with genuine specificity for once — the rep tied it directly to the prospect's own pathology rather than describing it generically: 'in your particular case, mobility is going to be the foundation of the whole training, because of the tight hips, because of the knee injuries, and the disc', and 'first month is going to be basically learning the basics of the movements, and also doing a lot of mobility work, for you to be more susceptible for more weights.' The prospect did not just accept it, he took it over and co-diagnosed: 'this will be the challenge. I know where is my problem. Not so much my knee, I think my hip, but it's like locked.' The rep met him — 'Believe me, everything comes from hips. This is the power of the whole body, core and hips' — and the prospect closed the loop, 'Yeah, so we're going to take care of that.' He then volunteered the Greece story unprompted when the rep mentioned travel, which is a prospect actively mapping the pillar onto his own failure history. Enthusiastic on both tests: volunteered reaction and tied to his own goal.

The most engaged nutrition reaction anywhere in this batch, and it ran in an unusual direction — the prospect pushed back toward more restriction, not less. Offered the standard weekly free day, he declined it: 'I think I will keep myself away from that for a while. Then when I see results, then I can cheat a little bit. Until then, I don't want to cheat, to be honest.' The rep handled that well and coached him off it — 'it's easy to go, okay, I'm going 100% in, and then you will fall off because it's very difficult to be 100%. It's damaging mentally' — which is exactly right for a man whose documented pattern is all-or-nothing collapse. The prospect then volunteered a self-observation that had not come up on the first call: cutting bread had changed his mood, 'I was like a more anxious and more nervous, getting upset', which the rep connected to carbohydrate crashes. The pillar was also personalised to his life rather than recited: 'Trevor is going to build a nutrition approach around your schedule and your lifestyle... whenever you're going to be on a business meeting or a dinner, you're going to know what to pick and how to eat.'

Delivered against his own failure history rather than in the abstract — 'You told me that you tried many times before and didn't do it fully. And that's why the coaching layer matters, because a lot of people can start, but the problem is staying consistent when life gets busy' — closing with 'when work gets crazy, or motivation dips, or life gets in the way, you don't fall off like before.' The response was firm but short: 'No, I should not. I would not. No, I would not. I don't want to', then 'it sounds pretty good for me, yes.' Scored accepted on the pillar itself. The enthusiasm for accountability had already been spent earlier and more powerfully, in Phase 5, where the rep asked for a mandate and got one: 'do I have your permission to hold you accountable to all the things that you said that are important to you?' / 'Yes, you should hold me accountable for that. Because that's what I'm here for.' And in Phase 4: 'Yeah, but I need as well. I think that's why I'm here with you.' Of the three pillars this is the one he had already bought before it was presented.

anchors.raw: 9K is not a small amount, even if we know we have good salaries here in Denmark. But either how, 9K is a lot of money, to be honest... Even for Denmark, we have a good salary and we have a good lifestyle, but...
anchors.note: Double-sided and the rep used the right side. The prospect volunteers that Danish incomes are good, which removes the affordability excuse, and then insists the number is still large. The rep did not argue with the size, he changed the shape — stepping to the six-month tier and offering instalments — which is the correct response to a price objection that is about magnitude rather than capacity.

anchors.raw: it's about decision what I make, you know, I make, I make deals all, all, all day, making deals and making the right things... I know the salespeople, you know, I'm also a sales guy.
anchors.note: The most important anchor on the call and the one that was read backwards. A self-identified dealmaker and salesman is comfortable transacting large sums, which supports the price — and is also the reason he will not wire money to an unverified foreign vendor, and the reason he recognises and resents pressure tactics. Every subsequent event on this call flows from this one fact, and the rep treated the resulting caution as fear rather than as professionalism.

anchors.raw: Either I choose you, and I go with you for a certain amount, even if I find another chance or somebody else... Either with you, either with somebody else. I need to do it anyhow.
anchors.note: He is buying the category, not the brand. That is good news for intent and bad news for price — an interchangeable vendor cannot hold a premium, and it also explains why verification became the deciding step. Nothing on either call established why Trevor specifically rather than any competent coach, and this statement went entirely uncontested.

anchors.raw: I think I watch, what's the guy's name? Trevor... I think I watch it for the past three months, two months... he's doing a good job. You can see on him and he's having his good physique... if Trevor can do it, why we cannot do it? He's not a superhuman.
anchors.note: The instructive counter-example to the rest of the batch. In the Jorge Fernández and Andy calls the free content substituted for the paid offer and killed the deal; here two to three months of the same content built belief and brought the prospect to the call warm, already owning kettlebells and already changing his diet. The difference is that this prospect concluded he could not execute it alone, and the free version had already given him back pain. Worth noting for funnel strategy: the same asset converts or cannibalises depending entirely on whether the viewer is capable of self-coaching.

anchors.raw: when you finish the six months and you feel like you would still need another six months, you can always top it up, but it won't be an additional 6K. It's going to be 3K.
anchors.note: An anchor Primal created rather than one the prospect brought. It establishes that twelve months of coaching can cost $9,000 or $6,000 plus $3,000 — the same total — but it also tells the prospect the ongoing rate is half the entry rate, which invites the question of why the first six months are priced at double. It is not in the documented offer and needs a decision: either it is a real retention mechanic and should be priced deliberately, or it should not be quoted.

anchors.raw: So the best one, I would say it's just to pay in half. So 3,000 now and 3,000 30 days later, we can split it up also in three or six pay, but that's gonna have like an additional interest on that... with three pay, it's going to be three times of 2,300... Of six pay, it's going to be six times 1,200.
anchors.note: Logged as an anchor because of what the prospect then agreed to. He chose monthly — 'I pay a month, I use a month' — while describing the deal as 'the six K'. Monthly is the six-payment plan, which totals $7,200, a 20% premium. Nobody reconciled the two numbers on the call. Whatever else happens on the follow-up, this needs correcting before payment, or the first invoice will contradict the handshake. Also worth noting that the half-now/half-at-30-days option matches the sanctioned structure and the three- and six-payment plans do not.

anchors.raw: now, after I finish with you, I will take the kettlebells and do something.
anchors.note: Behavioural rather than verbal evidence of intent: kettlebells already bought, training already started, diet already changed two weeks before any sales contact, and a plan to train immediately after the call ends. This is a prospect who acts before he is sold to, which is the strongest buying signal in the batch and part of why the handshake came easily.

unmet_demand.want: Verification material about the company and the coach before releasing money — 'information about the company that you are working with, your company, Trevor's', plus independent evidence: 'I think you have also some people who are satisfied or not satisfied with your job... I will check multiple places.'
unmet_demand.why_unmet: Nothing exists to send. The rep's response was to ask the prospect what he needed — 'What kind of information would you need?' — which shows there is no standard verification pack. For a business selling $6,000 to $9,000 engagements remotely and internationally, the absence of a one-click entity, credentials and references document is a straightforward positioning gap, not a product limitation. The proof almost certainly exists; it is simply not assembled or sendable, and in its place the rep offered a $100 deposit, which made the trust problem worse.

unmet_demand.want: A reason to choose Primal specifically rather than any competent coach — implied by 'Either with you, either with somebody else.'
unmet_demand.why_unmet: Trevor was described throughout as the delivery mechanism (he will build the plan, he will review your videos, you get his number) and never as the reason. No credentials, no results, no client outcomes, no differentiation from the alternatives the prospect said he would consider. The prospect's own belief in Trevor came entirely from watching free content, and the rep never built on it. This is the same positioning gap recorded against the Jorge Fernández call, and here it is the upstream cause of the verification demand.

unmet_demand.want: Clear, written payment terms he could hold to — he asked directly, 'What about the, how is the payment terms?'
unmet_demand.why_unmet: The terms were quoted verbally, three structures at once, and the option he selected was never priced back to him. He agreed to 'the six K' on a monthly schedule that totals $7,200. Nothing was sent in writing, no schedule was confirmed, and no agreement document was mentioned. The capability exists; the artifact does not.

unmet_demand.want: Confidence that loaded ballistic kettlebell training is safe for a compressed disc, a subluxing knee, a locked hip and two years of hypertension at 105 kg.
unmet_demand.why_unmet: Across two sessions and roughly 64 minutes, no clinician was mentioned by either party and no clearance question was asked. The mobility promise is real and well targeted, but it is a training promise, not a clinical one, and the prospect has already produced new back pain training unsupervised. There is no screening step anywhere in the process, so whether the programme can safely load this body remains unknown to everyone involved — including the rep who has now shaken hands on six months of it.
